claims.text: The initial FeNiCrCoCu coating is an FCC solid solution.
The coating is initially defect-free or has low dislocation density.
The stacking-fault energy of FeNiCrCoCu increases significantly between approximately 600 K and 900 K.
Increasing stacking-fault energy suppresses stacking faults and deformation twins.
Increasing stacking-fault energy suppresses partial-dislocation formation.
Suppression of partial dislocations and twins temporarily increases the elastic modulus.
Suppression of partial dislocations and twins produces dislocation starvation.
Above 900 K, thermal energy overcomes a lattice-distortion barrier and triggers rapid lattice disorder.
An FCC-to-HCP transformation begins above 900 K in the indented FeNiCrCoCu coating.
Amorphization begins above 900 K in the indented FeNiCrCoCu coating.
Negative or near-zero stacking-fault energy at high-temperature local strain states drives the proposed FCC-to-HCP transformation or amorphization.
High-temperature lattice disorder facilitates HCP-nucleus formation.
The high-temperature process annihilates stacking faults and acts as mechanical annealing.
Mechanical annealing eliminates the dislocation network needed for work hardening.
The resulting amorphous or HCP-rich surface layer has low shear strength.
High adhesion between the disordered surface layer and the indenter causes the friction coefficient to spike.
Amorphization causes the sharp loss of hardness and wear resistance and produces flow-like deformation.
At 300 K and 600 K, deformation is dominated by partial dislocations and twinning.
At 1200 K, the coating reaches maximum friction, minimum hardness, extensive HCP transformation or amorphization, and catastrophic wear failure.
Artificially suppressing FCC-to-HCP transformation should prevent both the friction spike and sharp hardness drop at 900 K and 1200 K.

contradictions.description: The account first says stacking-fault energy increases with temperature, but then invokes negative or near-zero stacking-fault energy above 900 K to drive the transition. No reversal or local-strain dependence is quantified to reconcile these statements, and the cited SFE record places negative SFE at cryogenic rather than high temperature.
The proposed 600–900 K stage suppresses partial dislocations and deformation twins, whereas the predicted outcome says deformation at 600 K is dominated by partial dislocations and twinning.

The hypothesis allows either FCC-to-HCP transformation or amorphization to cause the high-temperature response, but the experiment suppresses only FCC-to-HCP transformation. Persistence of the response could therefore remain consistent with the stated amorphization branch rather than decisively falsifying the overall hypothesis.
